utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Gotovina et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. First of all, the Chamber would like to convey its best wishes to everyone in and around the courtroom. We hope that the technical difficulties with which we started are not exemplary for what will be our future in 2010. After a relatively long break, the Chamber would like to inquire whether there are any procedural matters to be raised with urgency. We are not aware of any. I do not see anyone jumping up. So, therefore, I would like to ask the Markac Defence whether it's ready to call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are ready, Your Honour. Our next witness will be Ms. Snjezana Bagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Bagic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can hear me in a language understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Bagic, before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that will you speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is handed out to you by Madam Usher. I would like to invite toy make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bagic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bagic, are you the only one in this courtroom at this moment who is deprived of the best wishes of the Chamber for this year. I -- the Chamber would like to wish you all the best for 2010. You will now be examined by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac. Mr. Mikulicic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Bagic.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you please give us your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: My name is Snjezana Bagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bagic, given that we both speak the same language, I would just like to remind you that for the benefit of our interpreters we try to speak as slowly as possible and please try and make a pause between my question and your answer. Thereby we shall facilitate the work for both our interpreters and the court reporter. Ms. Bagic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before that, I would like to kindly ask the Registry to put up the document 3D00957.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You're going to see the document which is actually a statement of yours. You remember that in October last year you gave a statement to the Defence team of Mr. Markac. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But only -- yes, now I see the text of my statement on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go to the last page of the statement, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We're going to show you the last page which contains a signature, and I would kindly ask to you identify it. In the right-hand corner, you see a signature. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bagic, when you gave this statement and when you answered the questions, did you speak the truth to the best of your recollection and gave correct answers about all the events that were being discussed?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke the truth, and I described the events to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you these same questions today that were asked at the time when you gave your statement, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bagic, during yesterday's proofing for today's testimony after reviewing your statement, you have noticed certain correctness, incorrectness; for example, you noticed that the date is the 29th of October, 2009. However, that's the date on which you actually signed the statement, whereas, the interview was conducted on the 23rd of October, which you noted in your additional statement. Another amendment was done in paragraph 7 of your statement that you're referring to Article 9 instead that should be Article 2. Were those corrections the ones that you pointed out to us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are the these corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Registrar please show us the supplemental statement dated the 10th of January of this year, with all these corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bagic, do you recognise your signature in the lower left corner?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... do we need the supplemental information sheet? I mean, the two corrections have been put on the record by the answers given --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... in fact now, Your Honour, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we can do without.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Apart of these two corrections that we have just mentioned, is there anything else that you would like to change or amend or point out to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to tender Ms. Bagic's statement into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure all of the steps have been taken for 92 ter. I may have missed them, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think before the supplemental information sheet was referred to --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1911, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have prepared a summary of Ms. Bagic's statement. And with your indulgence and after I explained to her the purpose and the importance of this summary, I would like to read it out. Mrs. Snjezana Bagic is a lawyer by profession. At the moment, she is the judge of the court. She graduated from the Faculty of Law in Zagreb in 1983. Throughout her career she was involved in legal affairs in the economy, in the judiciary, and in legislative bodies. For example, she worked as a judge at the county court in Zagreb. She was an advisor at the Ministry of Justice. She was the secretary of the Ministry of Justice; deputy minister; head of the office for the cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal and the ICJ at The Hague; and also head of the legislative office of the government of the Republic of Croatia. Ms. Bagic personally took part in drafting the bills of numerous laws in the area of the property law, and, subsequently, in the preparation of the government decree and the Law on Temporary Acquisition and Management of specific property which, in fact, limited the rights of the individuals who had left the territory of the Republic of Croatia before, during, and after Operation Storm. The reasons for adopting this regulation were twofold: Primarily, there was a need to accommodate people, a large number of returnees, expelled people and refugees from other parts of Croatia as well as from abroad; and the second reason for passing this regulation was the need for -- provide protection for the abandoned property and to be protected from devastation, which was objectively possible and feasible only by having it temporarily under the jurisdiction --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, having it put into use and residential use.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This regulation did not -- did not affect property rights. Therefore, we are not talking here about confiscation of property, as was sometimes untruthfully described by people who were not fully familiar with the content of this regulation. The owners of the abandoned properties under this regulation had their property rights limited within the function of ownership, which was in line with the provisions of the constitution of the Republic of Croatia and which later turned out to be a legitimate move through the ruling of the European Court for Human Rights in Strasbourg. This court, through its rulings, established that the restriction of the ownership rights had been done with a legitimate aim and in the interest of providing for the displaced persons, but it made a note that certain flaws were detected on the part of Croatia, which is to provide compensation for those who are unable to use their own property. This was the summary of Ms. Bagic's statement. With your leave, Mr. President, I would now like to move on with my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bagic, today you work as a judge at the constitutional court of the Republic of Croatia. In brief, can you please describe to the Chamber and to everyone in this courtroom what is actually the role of the constitutional court within the government structure of the Republic of Croatia, and is this role today different from the one that existed in 1996, 1997, and the subsequent years and also before and during the Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am the judge with the constitutional court. I took up this duties on the 7th of December, 2006. This role hasn't changed either during the time of the Operation Storm or today. It is prescribed by the constitution of the Republic of Croatia and is elaborated more in detail on the constitution -- in the constitutional law of Croatia. It is believed that the constitutional court of Croatia has jurisdiction over constitutional courts which have the broadest jurisdiction compared to other European countries. However, I would like to highlight two functions which in my mind are most important. That is, abstract supervision and practical supervision. We are overseeing both the constitutionality of laws and bylaws and enactments and see that they are in line with the constitution. In addition to this abstract supervision, the constitutional court renders rulings on individual cases, whether they be judicial or administrative, but eventually they have to end up before a court, whether such ruling has violated any human or civic rights enshrined in the constitution. So this constitutes a constitutional complaint, and in that complaint the court specifies whether any such right had been violated or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. And this is a prelude to the question that I'm going to ask you later during our conversation. Just another detail in connection with the position of the constitutional court: Is the position of the constitutional court in the system of judicial power part of the judicial power something like a supra appeals court, or is the position of the constitutional court defined differently?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: It's defined differently. The constitutional court considered -- [French on English Channel] ... regular court even though it is called a constitutional court. So unfortunately, frequently, even among professionals, this is mixed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have problems with the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I hear a switch from English to French and from French to English rather frequently on Channel 4.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apologies from the French booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think matters have been corrected. We can proceed. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Ms. Bagic, we had some technical problems so I will ask you to repeat your answer from the part when you said that the constitutional court is actually not part of the regular judicial authorities but ...

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: The constitutional court is not part of the judiciary authorities. In judiciary practice, it is considered to be an intermediate body or the so-called fourth authority. And why? Because with the power of its constitutional jurisdictions through the decisions which it can make, it can supervise both the judiciary and the -- judiciary authorities and the legislative authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bagic, we will now go back to your career that you were focussed on during the 1990s, during the previous century, when you worked in the Ministry of Justice and held various positions there. We have mentioned in the summary of your statement, and I will ask you to expand on this, that you took part in the preparation of certain draft laws and league regulations. Can you describe to us in brief what procedure this was. How is a law drafted, or a legal regulation, in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: I will try. I will attempt to be as brief as possible. This is correct. In the Ministry of Justice, I started working there in 1991, and -- in the administration of land and property affairs, and I mainly worked in preparing and drafting regulations that had to do with civil law. If you allow for me a digression: We are talking here about the period of transition in the Republic of Croatia from the moment of its independence which implied the change of the entire social system and the shift from the social property to private property and the democratic system of the Republic of Croatia where the entire legislation needed to be changed at some point. So it was a quite hectic period in the legislation sense. And for jurists and lawyers it was very interesting but also very challenging. As for the preparation of regulations, when a certain regulation or a law is prepared and drafted, as a rule, a body or a ministry within the remit of which work these affairs come, has to draft it. So, for example, the laws that have to do with railways are part of the duty of the Ministry of Transport. And what had to do with legal affairs was the duty of the Ministry of Justice. Within the Ministry of Justice, the part or the department of the Ministry which was in charge was the one whose duty it was generally. For example, the administration for land had to prepare the regulations that had to do with civil law regulations. As the state administration, especially, certain departments did not have a sufficient number of lawyers who could do this; I'm talking in particular about laws which were absolutely new, such as the Law on Property, the Law on Asset Seizure, and so on. We had to establish working groups that were made up of professionals such as professors from the faculty law, or colleagues from Courts, from the bar association, and so on; and then these groups would prepare the draft laws. And finally once the text of such a law was drafted, so that it had the form of a draft law, the Ministry of Justice or another state body would send it to the government of the Republic of Croatia which would then discuss it in its professional bodies. It would harmonise it with other regulations because other ministries could also have some observations. If some regulations related to their remit of work, the constitutional court would also say whether this was in accordance with the constitution and other laws; and after all these discussions and discussions within the government, such a draft law would be adopted and then it would be sent as the proposal of the government to the Croatian parliament for further discussion and eventual possible adoption. Now, as for the further procedure of passing laws within the Croatian parliament, as a rule, the discussion related to two readings: First of all, it would be read as draft law; and then finally as a bill, meaning the final proposition of a law. So the specific bodies of the parliament would read it, and then a Plenary Session would also hold a discussion when the MPs would voice their own proposals, and after the end of this discussion they would voted for adoption of a draft law or it would be turned down. Fortunately, most often a draft law is adopted, then it's sent back to the government to explain why this would be adopted or not, and then again return it to the parliament in the form of a final bill. And the dead-line for this was six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation. We won't go further into the procedure itself. So it seems to me that you already answered, but let us clarify this once again. The entire procedure which you explained, the procedure about the adoption of a law, seems to be a lengthy one. How long did it last on average?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to say anything specific considering that this depended not only on the importance and length of the text of the law. However, most often, I would say that, on average, this would last between eight and ten months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, if, for the functioning of the state, there was a need to regulate a specific area with an urgent procedure in the Croatian structure of power, there is also a different procedure when the government may adopt the so-called decrees. Can you just explain to us in brief what the procedure was in such cases?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: I will try. Yes, the government has the power which is defined by the constitution to adopt decrees which have the power of laws. If you allow me, there is just one difference or let me clarify something. The government regularly has the power to adopt decrees and decree laws. They are regularly adopted for implementation of laws. What are you asking me about now is another kind of decrees; these are the so-called decree laws, and the government may adopt them on the basis of the constitutionally defined power that it has. It's a possibility that is allowed that the government may adopt such decrees and regulate certain areas with such decree laws, except certain issues that have to deal with basic human rights and liberties or the structure of the government bodies more at the state level and the local level. So the government, when passing these decree laws, refers to a -- this regulation of the constitution. I think I will -- if I say it's Article 87 of the constitution, I hope I am citing the right one. So the government might regulate issues relating to the Croatian parliament, and one of these issues has to do with the current economic policy. These decree laws, according to the constitution and according to this law, have limited effect, and they cease to be valid after one year, unless the parliament changes it with a law that has identical or similar contents even before the expiry of 12 months. So the government does have the power to pass these regulations which we call decree laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please see P476.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bagic, the subject of the -- this is a decree of the Government of the Republic of Croatia, which was adopted at a session on the 31st of August, 1995, and it's a decree on Temporary Takeover and Management of certain property. Do you have any personal knowledge of this decree? And do you know the temporal and logical contexts in which it was adopted?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this. Namely, it's always good to recall and here, in connection with what I said, it is mentioned that the decree is passed on the basis of this authority of the government, and it was adopted at the government session on 31st of August, 1995. If you deem it necessary, I can explain the context in more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you personally take part in drafting the text of this decree?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Because, I had previously taken part in the preparations and drafting of a law that had the exact same name. It was the Law on Temporary Takeover and Management of certain property.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If, for a second, we could see, D427, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bagic, I will show you now an exhibit which is already in evidence. And this is the draft law which was submitted to the parliament of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would ask the Registrar if we could please move to page 3D00-0911; that is, the explanation of the final draft of this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the left-hand side of the monitor you can see this explanation of the final bill, which says that the Chamber of Deputies of the Assembly of the Republic of Croatia at its 26th session on the 4th of July, 1995, adopted the conclusion accepting the bill on the Temporary Takeover and Management of certain property. If we look at the temporal sequence, then we can see as this was on the 4th of July, 1995, when the Chamber of Deputies adopted this bill, it was probably drafted earlier. Can you remember when exactly this bill on the Temporary Takeover and Management of certain property was submitted to the Croatian parliament?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, this bill was submitted to the parliament for discussion in the month of June, and it was adopted as a proposal of the Croatian government. It was submitted to the parliament for discussion. And then, depending on its agenda, it discussed it and adopted it at this session held on the 4th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And now the procedure in the parliament which you have described for us would follow. The first reading, second reading, sending it back to the government, and so on and so forth, and a this is a procedure that requires some time, of course. However, in the meantime, what happened was that the government --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we could now return to the previous document. And that is P476.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That the government at its session held on the 31st of August, that is to say before the parliament adopted this law, passed a decree on the temporal takeover and manage of property with the same text that was previously submitted to the parliament as a bill. Could you please describe to us now what were the circumstances that actually stimulated the government to react in this manner?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: I will try. If you allow me, I would first go back to the period that preceded the drafting of this bill. Namely, I have already said that at the time I was working in the Ministry of Justice in the administration for property affairs and since the early 1990s I would say since the year 1990 onwards when the Republic of Croatia became independent from the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and there were big changes in all the newly established states, the pressures for the population to move out had already begun because the population was moving to the countries of their ethnic origin. Why am I mentioning this? Because in the property administration there were many citizens who would come from Vojvodina - later on also from Bosnia and Herzegovina - particularly from the areas around Banja Luka, who had houses or apartments there, others types of property and which they would exchange with citizens from the Republic of Croatia. And they -- there was an increasing number of these contracts on exchange which could not really be implemented. I can only talked about citizens who did acquire some immovable property in the Republic of Croatia. As I already said, new regulations were being drafted. The newly established countries had not regulated their relations. And the issue was whether the signatures and the taxation that were determined in other countries were now valid or not. There was a need to react to that, and the Ministry of Justice would give its approval in terms of the validity of these documents originating from other countries. And after the Operation Flash in the spring of 1995 in the area of Eastern Slavonia, there were more people who abandoned property. It was not just exchange but people would just leave. The property was abandoned. There was plunder. There was destruction. And really there was an issue how to regulate this area legally in order to protect and preserve the property on the one hand, and on the other, help the citizens who, by selling or buying property or exchanging property, wanted to really exercise their property rights. The situation significantly changed because in the month of August, after the Operation Storm, the -- the quantity of property that was left behind, it was abandoned, whether the citizens left certain areas because they had been temporarily occupied or they now, after the liberation, went to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or to Bosnia and Herzegovina the problems really increased. It was clear that the property was abandoned, that things were being stolen, destroyed, plundered; and there was an urgent need to maintain order. I have to emphasise that the local authorities or the competent bodies in these areas were not capable concerning this phenomenon of the abandonment of property to react in a proper manner and protect this property. This was also connected with another fact that with the increase of people abandoning their properties, the number of other people, refugees, who were left without property arrived in Croatia and we faced the problem of providing accommodation for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What you told us now, Ms. Bagic, was actually part of my next question, which is: What was actually ratio legis of adopting such a law with the identical wording? For that purpose, will you please look at D8 -- 1823. That's the minutes from the 262nd closed session of the Government of the Republic of Croatia held on the 31st of August, in which members of the government explained the rationale underlining the adoption of this regulation. First of all, let me ask you: Did you attend this government session on the 31st of August, 1995, when this decree was adopted?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Your Honours, please. It seems that we have a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that we have some problems with the marking of the documents. Therefore, I would kindly ask the Registry to find the document, 05015. 65 ter -- yes, now we have it on our screens. Can we please move to page 3 in Croatian. That's 0614-2854.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bagic, I'm going to point out to you to the statement of Mr. Nikica Valentic, who says as follows: "Let's move to item 1, item 1 A and B, before I give the floor to the vice-president Misetic, who had coordinated work on this law -- and I'm talking about the Law on the Temporary Takeover, the second reading, and the draft decree with the identical wording, I would like to draw the government's attention to the fact that this is one of the most important documents that the government is to adopt both from the legal and the factual point of view and with respect to political implications. "As you may have seen, it is actually about the necessity to protect the property which de facto lost its proprietor, the property worth billions, the property which is under no one's protection and which is largely because of that partly burned and robbed, and unless this property is not placed under the protection, it is practically impossible to protect this property in this large area. We are fully aware of possible political implications, and that is why we opted for the solution that we deem to have factual, political, and legal justification. That is why I would like to ask Vice-President Misetic to elaborate on this law and this decree; and maybe I should explain why we decided to come up with the this decree?" "We have analysed the constitutional grounds thoroughly, and we think that this decree does not contravene the constitution. But since we will have a draft law in procedure before the parliament, the parliament may, in its next or in the session after their next session, pass the law, thus abrogating the degree; however, the decree is clearly standing in lieu of the law before the law is passed." After that, Mr. Bosiljko Misetic, the vice-premier at the time, offered the following explanation and he says as follows on the next page that -- this was about the property divided into several categories, and there were also several categories of citizens, and then he lists in the second paragraph the property of the citizens of Croatia who on the 18th of August, 1995, that is, the date on the aggression on the Croatia had left Croatia. The second type of property relates to physical and legal persons, citizens of Serbia and Montenegro whose property is located in Croatia. And the third category refers to the property in the occupied regions which in the Croatian operation for the liberation of these regions their proprieties left Croatia. Bosiljko Misetic went on to say that the purpose of adopting this law is to manage this property in a good way, in order to avoid irreparable damage caused to the property and to provide in -- by properly using and managing this property, ensure that a large number of citizens, primarily Croats, who had been expelled from other parts of Yugoslavia by the Serbs. And on the next page, this is what Mr. Misetic says, line 10 from the top -- seventh line from the top, this is what he says: "The final proposal of the coordinating bodies for internal affairs and of all" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters didn't get on their screens the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but the -- at line 17 the sentence wasn't completed when it was read what Mr. Bosiljko Misetic said. It was primarily Croats who had been expelled from other parts of Yugoslavia by the Serbs would benefit from this property is how the sentence ends in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree with that to be the text of that sentence, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me see. The final proposal ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There also was an issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask you, given that you took part in the preparation of the law and that you have now seen how the vice-premier at the government session explained the rationale underlining this adoption, according to your understanding and the principles that you were guided by in drafting the law, is this how this procedure was conducted?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It seems to me that this corresponds with the procedure, how this was done. And I think that between these two laws there was a decree. Mainly jurists from the ministry, from the faculty of law, and other ministries of the government of Croatia -- of Croatia took part in this, and they had to analyse which of these provisions would be constitutionally accepted and well founded. We were aware that our constitutional, no matter how recent it was, and we were practically learning about private property and what guarantees are attached to it. However, this is not an absolute right. It is subject to certain limitations, but that could only be done by means of a law under the circumstances which, for example, require the protection of the Republic of Croatia. Secondly, when a law or a decree were being drafted, we never discussed seizure of ownership or the right to property in any way whatsoever. But since this was abandoned property and its owners were away, we came up with the idea of a limited use of property. We just then had to find an acceptable legal framework which would incorporate this kind of limited restriction of property rights, in a way by allowing third persons who are also part of the law to temporarily use such property.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now ask the Registry to show us Exhibit P476, which is the decree itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said, Ms. Bagic, that ownership is a category which is defined by the Croatian laws and that this -- this decree did not derogate or abrogate the ownership but only limit it?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am not sure whether your whole answer was completely interpreted. Can you please repeat what kind of limitation was envisaged by this decree?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: This decree put this property under temporary management. When we are talking about individual property rights, it affected ownership because it allowed for a possibility for this property, pursuant to the decision of competent bodies and commission, to be given to third parties for temporary use. This was a targeted group of people that we are talking about here. These are expellees, refugees, families of the fallen fighters from the homeland war, and other such individuals. I will try, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at Article 2 of this decree, paragraph 2, which reads: "From the date this decree comes into force, property situated in the territory of the Republic of Croatia owned by the individuals who left the Republic of Croatia after August 17th, 1990, property in the occupied area of the Republic of Croatia which is situated in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro) or in the occupied area of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and which has not been used personally by the owners since the day they left." So here we see the definition of both the property and the individual relating to it, and it stretches back to the 17th of August, 1990, which is the date of the aggression against Croatia which was referred by Mr. Misetic at the government session. In terms of this decree, the term "property" shall mean all movable and non-movable property. From the point of view of legislative solution, can you please explain this?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: The temporary administration as this defines it, included immovable property, meaning houses and land, and also the movable property that belonged to such property, because there were situations when somebody would just come somewhere, enter, take machinery or tools, steal them, misappropriate another person's property, in other words. So the reason, the purpose was that when immovable property was given for use to certain categories of persons who were meant to live there and also make a living, then in order to protect the property to prevent the misappropriation or theft in this way by allowing these people to use it, and this is why the decree covered both immovable and moveable property.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us now look together on the next page in the Croatian text, Article 4, which envisages the establishing of commissions in municipalities or towns which had concern tasks. Can you tell us anything about the task of these commissions, in terms of this decree or bill which it later became?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Namely, the assessment was that the local authorities and the local population would best be able to recognise what property this related to and implement this law so that in towns and municipalities, commissions were set up which primarily had to list the property in question, the property that was covered by this law, and that was to be considered abandoned. In addition to listing the property, establishing what is the property that this law or decree covers, they had additional authority, and that was to give this property for use to categories which are listed in Article 5 - I think I already mentioned this - these were targeted groups, because we are talking about circumstances where we had a refugee crisis at the time in the Republic of Croatia. We had a huge inflow of refugees of returnees who had no accommodation. And this is why this decree and law explicitly related only to these categories of people. All other categories of people could not be covered by the decree or it would be illegal if that was done. Likewise, when the commissions made the decisions to give property for use to these categories, they were also obliged to make an Official Note about the condition of the property at the moment when it was temporarily allowed for use to temporary users. The work of the commissions was directed by the ministry of renewal which had to check if everything was working all right. If there were any problems between various local authorities, if there were any difficulties in the interpretation and the implementation of this decree by certain of these commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So we see in Article 4 in the penultimate paragraph that one representative each from the Ministry of Development and Reconstruction, Ministry of Reconstruction, Ministry of the Interior, Minister of Labour and Social Welfare, Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry, Office of the Government of the Republic of Croatia for Expelled Persons and Refugees, the public legal office, the municipal or town government, as well as other representatives, if necessary, would be appointed to the commission. Can you tell us what was the reason because of which the decree envisaged the composition of the commission in this way, why there would be members of the state ministries on the one hand and also representatives of the local community?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: This was done because it seemed necessary at the time, and it seemed to be a pragmatic solution, because on the one hand the representatives of the local community were the ones who best knew the circumstances in their own areas; and on the other hand, the state was about to take over the administration of the property. So if it did so, it also had to take measures to ensure the implementation of all this and the protection of this property. This was also an extraordinary and a complex situation, and it was deemed necessary that all the relevant government bodies, the ministries, should also have their representatives in these commissions. On the one hand, the reason was to protect the interests of the state and the protection of the property by exercising the role of the state; and on the other hand, so that these representatives of the highest body, that is to say the ministries, could implement the decree or law as best as possible in cooperation with the representatives of the local community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You have already said that the property was listed. And in Article 4, in the third paragraph, it is mentioned that the list of property is to be submitted to the ministry of development and reconstruction which would then take care of the property. Ms. Bagic, what was actually the purpose for a ministry to keep the record of the property which was in this way placed under the administration of the state?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: It seemed necessary to centralise the lists and to have unified records in one place so that by such inspection and supervision, all possible disharmony, abuse, and problems could be prevented and so that this could be regularly checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In Article 5 of this decree, it is mentioned that the commissions referred to make decisions by which they would allow the expelled persons and refugees to use such property and that appeals could be filed with the Ministry of Justice against these decision but which would not stay the execution of the decisions. From your experience, were there any cases when the ministry would decide on these appeals? How frequent was this phenomenon as far as you remember?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, appeal with the Ministry of Justice was allowed. In my experience, as far as I can remember, there were some complaints or appeals submitted to the Ministry of Justice. However, the number of such complaints was not great, because they were just authorised persons who could submit them, and there weren't too many of such complaints against the decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So the Ministry of Justice was the one who decided about these complaints?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there any other form of protection as regards the decision of the Ministry of Justice about the complaint?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: When the decree was implemented and the Law on the Temporary Takeover of Property was implemented, the Law on General Administrative Procedure was also implemented. So if there was a party that was dissatisfied, it could file an appeal to an administrative court and ask for the protection of its rights or try to overturn this decision in front of an administrative -- before an administrative court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This was the so-called court control of administration; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us look now at Article 7. It provides that persons who were given property for possession had to manage it well, protect it from third parties, and had all the authority that would belong to the owner himself or herself, and that they could utilise any income generated by the property for their own needs. Paragraph 2 provides that the persons who have been allocated the property for use could not dispose of the real estate which constitutes a part of the property, that is to say they could not sell it, exchange it, lease, rent, make it available for use by paying or non-paying parties, or incumber it with a mortgage or any other liability, and could not use the vehicles or cattle without the approval of the commission mentioned in Article 4 of this decree. And then, further on, it says that legal contracts which were concluded and that were contrary to this decree were invalid. Can you please comment on what this actually meant in practice and how it was implemented?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: This provision was aimed at reinforcing the protection of the rights of the owners by specifying quite clearly that the person who was allocated the property and who could be using it temporarily could not actually dispose of this property in any way, simply because this person was not the owner. On the other hand, when the person was temporarily using the property and possessed it for a temporary period, then the person was obliged to manage it as well as possible. It was also allowed because these persons had no income whatsoever and we were aware that these were mostly expelled persons and refugees, persons who were unemployed or were receiving social welfare, so if they could generate any income, then they were allowed to use this income for their own needs. And that then, because they were using and possessing this property, they had the right to prevent any attempts to use this property illegally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If it happened anyway that the person who was allocated the property for his or her use sold the property to a third party, what would be the validity of such a contract defining the sale?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of Article 7 it says that any such legal transactions would be considered null and void, so the owner could request that it be determined that such a legal transaction was null and void. It would be considered non-existent, but legal proceedings would have to be initiated in order to determine the fact that this transaction was null and void.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us look at Article 10 of this decree now. It says that if the owner of the property referred to in paragraph 1 of Article 2 returns to the Republic of Croatia within 30 days of this decree coming into force and seeks restitution, the commission, referred to in Article 4 of this law, shall quash the decision. Can you please explain for us this provision which mentions 30 days as a dead-line, and what was the rationale to envisage such a dead-line in the decree?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: The decree envisaged the 30 days dead-line, that is more or less one month, for the owner to return and seek restitution, that is to say the possession and in fact the use of his or her property. One could ask, especially from the perspective we have at this point of time and our later attempts to resolve the issue of property of refugees and expelled persons, whether this dead-line was too short or too long, how realistic was it. At the moment when the decree was drafted, the intention was to resolve the relations as soon as possible. So by setting up this dead-line, we wanted to allow the owners to return as soon as possible and seek the restitution so that people could come into possession of their property as soon as possible, and then the state would know what was the segment of the property that could still be temporarily administered by the state and used by the temporary users.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us look at Article 11 which says: "Ownership of the movable property referred to in Article 2 of this decree." And if we looked at Article 2, it's described there what this has to do with. It cannot be acquired by appropriation or occupation. Can you please comment on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I'm looking at the clock. We are close to 10.30. You are apparently starting with a new subject. If you would be able to finish that in two or three minutes, fine. If not, then I would suggest that we would leave it until after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: -- much more possible to continue after the break with this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then apart from that and before having the break, Mr. Mikulicic, reading your summary, I read - and I'm referring to page 6, line 18 and following - it says: "This regulation did not, did not affect property rights. Therefore, we are not talking here about confiscation of property as was sometimes untruthfully described by people who were not fully familiar with the content of this regulation." This is -- where do we find this in the statement which is here summarized? Because I had difficulties in finding any comment of this witness on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether other people described unfruitfully, people not being fully familiar with the content of there regulation. I had difficulties in finding this in the statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will come to that topic in my further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: -- examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question is where do I find it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I think literally you cannot find it in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where do we find it substantially?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, I think you cannot find it. You're right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you are mixing --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It was, rather, context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's not rather context; it's mixing in your own opinion in what is presented as a summary of a witness statement, which is not what this Chamber expects you to do. A summary is a summary of what is found in the witness statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and not your own comment on matters and your own implicit comment on familiarity from others - we do not know exactly who, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But I will go through that topic in further examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. But my observation is primarily a procedural one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. You are perfectly right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a break, and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you may proceed. If you enter into the area you earlier said you would like to deal with, that is, about whether or not the legislation affected the title of ownership, then I'd first like to verify whether there's any dispute about what this legislation, in formal terms, says about ownership, because it could well be that there's no dispute about certain matters. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the break, we quoted Article 11 of the decree, and I will reiterate it. It states that concerning the movable property from provision 2 of the Article, property rights cannot be enjoyed by virtue of occupation. This is what you were trying to tell us about the abandoned properties where some agricultural machinery was found as well as household appliances. Can you tell us what was the reason to specify this in the decree, that is to say that no property rights could be enjoyed by virtue of occupation of such movable property?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: This provision pertains only to movable property. It has nothing to do with immovable property. Why did the legislature deem it necessary to make this distinction? Because our law about property rights is the basic law which prescribes title of ownership that was in force at the time. It stipulated that that immovable property cannot be considered to change ownership by virtue of occupation. However, no such a provision was found in the law concerning immovable property. Therefore, it was believed to be necessary to prevent such actions as well, in order for anyone to gain anyone's property by virtue of occupation, the property that was given to that particular person to use. That is why this particular provision was inserted into the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Article 14 of the decree states that there will be a separate law -- shall be issued concerning the ownership of property placed under administration pursuant to the provisions of this decree that has not been restored to its owner. What was the idea behind this provision?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: The decree and the law did not address the issue of ownership in the sense of taking away such property rights, save for the limitations -- save for the issue of use by a third person. Based on our previous experience, when there were swaps of property between those citizens moving among the different countries which came about as a result of the break-up of Yugoslavia, and even from today's standpoint, we believe that it was quite unrealistic that situation could be ascertained within the legal limit of 30 days. In order for the rightful owners to enjoy their rights and to use the properties involved, we wanted to regulate this segment as well by law in order to prescribe a way in which people could make use of such property in cases in which owners wanted to sell their property, change that for another piece of property, or do whatever with it they wished to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D689 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As we said, this decree came into force when it was published in the Official Gazette and adopted by the government on the 31st of August, 1995. Ms. Bagic, you see another document before you, which is a legal analysis of this decree drafted by the Centre for Human Rights of the UN. We can see that this draft was provided by Ms. Maida Pasic. It is dated the 23rd of October, 1995. First of all, I'd like you this [as interpreted]. Did you have occasion to see this document before?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I wanted to direct your attention to certain portions of the document through, some aspects of this legal analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hence, we should go to item 2 at page 3 in the Croatian; and item 2, page 1D40-0501 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In item 2 of this legal analysis, we find the following: "There is no legal basis for putting the property of citizens who are currently outside the territory of Croatia," referring to Article 2 of the decree. "Under the temporary governing of the Republic of Croatia, since the decree starts from a wrong supposition that the property in question is deserted. Namely, in order to consider a property deserted, it is necessary that its owner, in a doubtless way, expresses a will that he does not want to keep it anymore." Ms. Bagic, this seems to involve the legal qualification of an abandoned property. Do you agree with this interpretation drafted by the Centre for Human Rights of the UN?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: I do not. Because that type of property, in view of all of us who worked on that law and given the factual situation in that area, it was abandoned. It involved thousands of persons who had left that area to go to some other occupied parts of Croatia or to the FRY or other former Yugoslav republics, perhaps even Bosnia and Herzegovina. That property was vacant and there was no one to take care of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The issue of qualifying a piece of property as abandoned, is that a legal or a practical issue?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: A definition of an abandoned property can be a legal issue, but it must, as far as I'm concerned, be linked to the factual situation. Certainly, in individual cases, the owner can ask for a different qualification in order to prove that this was not an abandoned piece of property.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us go down item 2 in paragraph 4, which states: "It is obvious that the decree, de facto, implements the process of confiscating property in the spirit of revolutionary law. It represents not only the violation of basic legal provisions but also an attempt to implement a chauvinist policy and to legally regulate the ethnic cleansing which had taken place. It is also based on the abandoned "tradition" of the 50-year experience with a general act. All Serbs not currently living in the territory of Croatia are deprived of their report, regardless of the fact that the formal legal question of property is not mentioned." Ms. Bagic, as a person working on the law and decree, do you agree with this legal view?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: I do not. Because when the law and the decree were being worked on, we strove to be as careful as possible about the issue of property and its inalienability. That is to say the category of property and ownership rights should not be brought into question in terms of temporary use by third parties. I don't know whether I am allowed to add something else concerning this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: The term "confiscation of property" is used in the spirit of revolutionary law, based on the tradition of 50 years' experience. The Republic of Croatia, as a part of the former Yugoslavia, was a state with a Communist regime in force as well as socialism and public ownership. The institute of property confiscation was familiar to us, as such. Furthermore, in the period of transition in Croatia as well as in many other encounters of central and eastern Europe at the time, legislation was being drafted which would enable return of property once seized. There were 42 different pieces of legislation that was used in the former Yugoslavia to confiscate and take away property. One such law precisely went to property confiscation. Property was taken away from their rightful -- from the rightful owners, becoming publicly owned property.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Which period do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: I apologise if I am being unclear. It was at the time when property was taken away in the former Yugoslavia, right after World War II, starting with 1945 until 1958. It is believed that the procedure of taking away property was completed and its transfer to the public hands was rounded off by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you mean the period of confiscation when, after World War II, the socialist powers took away property from former owners?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does this decree have anything to do with that type of legal procedure which, at that time, was termed "confiscation"?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: It is my firm belief that it has nothing to do with it. I say so because at the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, the text you read says what the factual effect is, not what the legal basis for it is. So, therefore, to compare the confiscation legislation as it existed in previous periods to compare with this, where there is not even a suggestion that the ownership has been affected in a formal way doesn't make -- doesn't seem to make much sense, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honour, I was referring to the part of the text which says: "It is obvious that this decree, de facto, implements the confiscation of property in the spirit of revolutionary law."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, de facto.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not de jure, but de facto. That's exactly why I said that it might not be of great assistance to this Chamber to compare the legal basis of this piece of legislation with, if I could say, the Communist legislation. Because that's not what is suggested here. It's suggested here that it has a similar effect, that you couldn't enjoy your property anymore. That's at least how I read this comment, especially where it says that even the ownership is not even mentioned. There seems to be - but I'm also looking at you, Ms. Gustafson - is there any dispute about that formally, unlike what happened in the past, that formally the ownership is not directly affected by this piece of legislation?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a difficult time with the Prosecution saying that there is no dispute on this issue. I believe - and I'm looking at the transcript at the 92 bis ruling, this is at page 17615, line 20: "The Chamber relied on at 92 bis that Galbraith also testified about laws on confiscation of property which required those who had left Croatia to return within a short period of time or risk loosing their property." So there is -- and then if we look at Mr. Galbraith' testimony - this is at page 5129, beginning at line 21 - Mr. Galbraith testified that: "Croatian actions was to confiscate property of people who did not return in 30 days and then it would be settled. The plan was this would then be settled as part of the overall settlement of claims between Croatia and Yugoslavia in which these Croatian citizens who, in Tudjman's words, were "optanci," their property claims would be settled as part of an overall settlement, which, in effect, would give them nothing." Now that's the Prosecution's case in chief, and we're getting into -- in my opinion, getting into a semantics now about the definition of confiscation. And I think the prosecution's case in chief clearly was that people's -- there was a plan to take people's property. In the context of settlement of claims between Croatia and Yugoslavia, these people would receive no compensation. That was Mr. Galbraith' testimony. Now, de facto, de jure, et cetera, I think it's relevant evidence to show what was the intent of the drafters of the legislation - this witness apparently has knowledge of it - and we can argue later about what is or isn't confiscation, but confiscation was the word used by the Chamber on the 92 bis ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The mere use of the word "confiscation," of course, is not a decisive matter in this respect because I don't think that with Mr. Galbraith we went through all the legal technical aspects of what this legislation was. And when I earlier said de jure, de facto, that might exactly be the issue. And if the witness could tell us something about the intent but then in the full context. I never opposed against exploring that. I was just figuring out whether there's any dispute, whether this legislation, this piece of legislation, in its de jure effect, would have, as a consequence, that the ownership would be lost. Because that seems to be -- not be disputed. And, Ms. Gustafson, may I take it that if you rely on the testimony of Mr. Galbraith about confiscation that it's not in the technical sense but in the end effect the de facto result of what this legislation might have brought about?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's then proceed on this basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, just so -- for the record - and we have consulted about this - we're not sure how can you confiscate property de facto. I mean, either have you a legal ownership right in something and have been -- been given a compensation or denied or you haven't. I don't see how you can de jure not have something confiscated but de facto it has been confiscated. We can say you have been denied use of your property, but that's not confiscation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if do you that effectively for a longer period of time, it may not be confiscation in the technical term, but some people could look at this as having the effect of -- I mean, what's ownership? What's ownership if you can't enjoy the ownership of something?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is precisely confiscation de jure. You've had your property seized without compensation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it -- this seems to be a legal debate -- becomes a legal debate, and the only thing I was looking at is whether the technical way in which the ownership and the guardianship of matters abandoned or not abandoned or half abandoned by another entity, whether it was understood by the Prosecution and whether there's any dispute about that formal ownership would be affected by that legislation as it was adopted at the time. I'm not talking about the long-term political aims, et cetera, but -- and there seems to be no dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But just so that he with are all on the same page. The Prosecution's case, as far as we understand it, is that property was confiscated. Whether they dispute that title didn't change hands, that may be a different issue. But there is a dispute about whether there was confiscation. As -- using your definition, Mr. President, of seizure of property without compensation for an extended period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I am -- I was not, at that moment, giving the final legal definition on a matter. It might be that we -- but certainly -- I mean, the issue which seems to be clear, and I asked for the Prosecution's position in relation to this matter in order to avoid unnecessary hearing of evidence. Ms. Gustafson, not to say that the Prosecution has the last word, but anything you would like to add or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Mikulicic, may this serve as guidance for your further examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at item 4 of this document. It's on the next page in both versions, where it reads: "The decree of the government of the Republic of Croatia represents an act of discrimination against the citizens of Croatia since the universal declaration of human rights, (Article 13), and the international covenant of civil and political rights, (Article 12), explicitly foresee that 'everyone has the right to leave any country, including his own, and to return to his or her country.'" Ms. Bagic, in this decree that we have just been commenting upon, can you find any provisions testifying to the existence of discrimination against citizens of Croatia with regard to their return to the country?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot. This decree and the later law did not have that effect. It referred to the property of all citizens whose property was abandoned and not used personally by them, that the law and the decree did not have any discriminatory provision as was confirmed later by a Court in 1997 and also by subsequent case law by -- of the Court for Human Rights, the same was confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you therefore agree with this legal view as stipulated in item 4?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: No, I do not agree. I honestly don't understand on what basis they have drawn this conclusion, from which provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And now, finally, let's look at the conclusion of this legal analysis. It reads in the last paragraph: "Bearing in mind all the above-mentioned, it is obvious that this decree does not regulate the disposal of the -- the legally based disposal of the property but that it is -- it represents a biased act of the state which takes away the property in a way most similar to confiscation. This decree is violating numerous international norms, particularly Article 17, which says that everyone is in entitled to ownership than no one can arbitrarily be deprived of it. In addition, this decree opens the way for discrimination on the basis of national and ethnic background in its purest form. The decree is contrary to the constitution of the Republic of Croatia. Therefore, Croatia is bound to annul the decree immediately." Ms. Bagic, regardless of our previous discussion about the definition of "confiscation," we have here another term which is the seizure of property. How would you comment this decision to seize the property in a legal sense?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: With respect to what you have read to me now, I already said that I cannot understand or find the basis on which the author of this document reached such a conclusion; namely, neither in the preparation nor in the provisions of this decree and the later now nor in their implementation in practice can one conclude that the implementation of this decree, in practice, boiled down to the confiscation of property. I have -- feel the need to underline this once again. This provision does not imply the seizure or the taking away of the right of ownership. What we are dealing here is the limitation of ownership which we thought to be embedded in the law, and the purpose of it was to protect the interests of the Republic of Croatia. We put limitation only on one property right which is the disposal of ownership which he could not exercise. And why? Because, at that time, this property was abandoned; the owner wasn't using it; and there was the need to provide shelter for refugees and other displaced people. As I said, the constitutional court ruled on this in 1997. And later on, the same ruling was passed by the European Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to this topic now. I would like to ask you to look at this part of the conclusion which says that this decree implements the discrimination on the basis of national and ethnic background. Do you see any base for such an opinion?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. Because both the decree and the law speak about property, deserted property not used by the owners personally, irrespective of their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at document that we saw before, that's D427. That's a draft or a bill of the law submitted to the parliament of the Republic of Croatia in June on the temporarily taking over and governing of property. And also it contains the rationale for the provisions contained therein. In the Croatian version, can we please look at page 3D00-0911. In the English version that's page 9 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Here, the proposing party provides the rationale to the parliament for adopting this law, and they speak about the two reasons that were -- that they were driven by. And that is to protect the property from misappropriation, and, on the other hand, there was the need to provide accommodation for returnees in this property. However, towards the bottom of the page in the last paragraph, there is mention of a third reason and I would kindly ask you to listen to this. It is no less important the need to have in the formally occupied territories of the Republic of Croatia revitalise the economy which is impossible without proper professionals. How would you comment this specific reason that is stated here as the basis for adopting this law?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: In addition to these two fundamental reasons that we already discussed, i.e., the protection of the property and providing accommodation to refugees during the crisis, the refugees who had lost their property or their property was damaged, it was clear already at that point that the return of the population to the formally occupied territories and now liberated territories would not be possible without revitalisation of the economy in the area and without creating the conditions for employment. There was no electricity supply; industrial facilities were demolished et cetera. Therefore, there was no encouragements for the citizens to return because there were no jobs secured for them. That is why certain professionals were required to return there in order to get the economy going and thereby secure the return of the population who will be able to provide for themselves by earning for living. This was later introduced by introducing the Law of Social Welfare in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we now turn to the next page and look at another portion. Here, the second passage and first passage in English reads as follows: "I therefore propose the limitation of ownership rights and placing abandoned property that is not being used personally under administration and giving it to other persons for possession and use in order to preserve it, to secure the subsistence of other persons through its use, and to help the economic and social renewal of the previously occupied and now liberated areas of the Republic of Croatia." And now an it goes on to say: "It is undoubtedly in the interests of Republic of Croatia, so the conditions set out in Article 50, paragraph 2 of the constitution of the Republic of Croatia for the adoption of this law has been fulfilled." Can you just briefly tell us what Article 50, paragraph 2 of the constitution says with regard to the implementation and adoption of this decree?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Whenever we speak about property rights and the exercise of property rights, a question of the limit and constitutional acceptability of the use of this right is being posed. Article 50, paragraph 2, among other things, allows exceptionally and only under the law can property rights be restricted if it is necessary to protect the interests and security of the Republic of Croatia. The Government of Croatia, and for us, who, as legal experts participated in the drafting of this provision, and I'm talking both about the decree and the law, pursuant to Article 50, paragraph 2, we thought that that was an appropriate constitutional foundation, under the given circumstances when Croatia was in war, when we had a huge number of properties abandoned, that we had so many people who were expelled, we thought that it would be appropriate to limit the ownership rights by invoking Article 50, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the reference, the constitution of the Republic of Croatia has been admitted into evidence as Exhibit D1779. Can we now move to the next page where this is an explanation for Articles 5, 7, and 9 of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, it says also imposed are limitations with regard to the disposal of this property. This implies those powers that lege lata belong only to the owner of this property. That is why it is -- therefore, all legal transactions entered into by the person to whom the property had been given for use shall be null and void. And pursuant to Article 9, this property may be taken away from that person that had received it temporarily for use, if he acts contrary to the provisions of this law or does not exercise due care. These commissions that included the representatives of local communities, did they supervise or oversee how the people who were granted the use of the abandoned property exercise this right? How did they use it?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, one of the tasks of the commissions was to supervise within their respective remits whether the temporary owner was using it in accordance with the law. It was their duty to act if they received any report or a claim that the temporary owner was not using the property in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4, commenting on Article 8, it says that this law introduces only administration -- sequestration by the Republic of Croatia of the property, referred to in Article 2 of the law, which means that the owner of that property will not be stripped of his ownership. Article 50, paragraph 1 of the constitution is not applied. However, on the basis of Article 50, paragraph 2 of the constitution, his property right will be restricted. These restrictions on property rights are regulated by Article 8, paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move to the next page which -- where we have the explanation of our paragraph -- of Article 16. It's the bottom of the page in Croatian. That's right. That's item 9. And in English, can we also please move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Item 9, commenting Article 16. It reads: "Since the issues governed by this law were regulated de lege lata by the decree on the Temporary Takeover and Management of certain property ... adopted by the government of the Republic of Croatia as part of its legislative powers, the decree shall become null and void on the day this law enters into force." Ms. Bagic, this is a procedure, actually, that you described before when we have a law coming into force in lieu of a decree.
