utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the document D422.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is the Official Gazette of the Republic of Croatia in which laws and other regulations are published and in which this document of the 27th of September, 1995, it was published here. It was the law adopted by the Croatian parliament about the temporary taking over and administration of specified property, and recently we saw the bill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please see Article 11 of this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Which reads: "If the owner of the property, under Article 2, paragraph 1 of this law," that is to say, abandoned property, "returns to the Republic of Croatia and claims this property for his restitution and use within 90 days from the date of entering of this law into force, the commission, under Article 4 of this law, shall reverse the decision under Article 5 of this law." So we can see that the time-limit of 90 days is mentioned here, as compared to the decree which had the time-limit of 30 days. Can you please comment on that?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: The dead-line was expanded from 30 days, as in decree, to 90 days, because -- at least that's how it seems to me now from this point in time, because it turned out that it was not realistic that an owner could return within such a short time-span of 30 days and asked a restitution of his or her property. There were objective difficulties because there were great migrations of the population. One could not reach the owner because it was not known where the new address where he or she was residing was. The traffic between the countries was also difficult. So it seemed logical and necessary to extend the dead-line, and this is why, here in Article 11, this time-limit for claiming the restitution of property was extended to 90 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So this was happening, as we said, on the 27th of September, 1995, that is to say, a month after the decree had been adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now look at document P475.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is a law, the Law on Amendments to the law that we just had a look at, the Law on the Temporary Takeover and Management of certain property. The law was amended on the 23rd of January, 1996, that is to say, roughly five months after its adoption. And please, Ms. Bagic, focus on Article 1, paragraph 2, which says, it changes Article 11 of the law in terms of the time limitation and says: "The issue of returning in possession and use of property which is under the ownership of persons from Article 2 of this law will be regulated by the agreement on the normalisation of relations between the Republic of Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." So we can see that the dead-line of 90 days, which was envisaged by the previous law five months earlier, was declared null and void by this provision. And it is mentioned here that this issue would be regulated by the agreement on the future normalisation of relations between the Republic of Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Could you please comment on this provision of the Law on Amendments?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: During the implementation of this law, it turned out that whatever the dead-line was, that the dead-line was not realistic because there were such objective difficulties that one could not set any dead-line and then request the owner to request the restitution of his or her property. And perhaps the conclusions and impressions were wrong, so it was better to remove the dead-line and allow the owner to request restitution once he returns. That was one of the reasons. Another reason was that the two countries, the Republic of Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, had already been begun negotiations at the time. The relations were being re-established, and the issue of the return of refugees was a matter of interest of any country where they were, including also Bosnia and Herzegovina and not just the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It was a regional issue - not to say a regional problem - and only with mutual cooperation it could be resolved, the cooperation between two or later on three countries. Therefore, by this Law on Amendments to the previous law, this dead-line was abolished, and it was provided that the issue would be further regulated by the agreement on the normalisation of relations. Let us now look at this agreement on the normalisation of relations which is included in the document D412.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D412.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And just to find our bearings in time, the law that abolished the dead-line was passed in late January 1996, and it refers to the adoption of the agreement between the Republic of Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] could we please move further on in this document because the agreement on normalisation that I referred to is an integral part of this document. Unfortunately, I don't have this version in front of me, but ... Just a second, please. Yes. Now we see the right text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is the agreement on normalisation of relations between the Republic of Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia dating from the 23rd of August, 1996. Under Article 7 of this agreement --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Article 7 on the screen. It is on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It reads: "The contracting parties under -- shall ensure conditions for free and safe return of refugees and displaced persons to their places of residence or other places that they freely choose. The contracting parties shall ensure to these persons the return of their property or a just compensation." Ms. Bagic, can you please comment on this provision of paragraph 1 of Article 7 of the agreement as compared to the earlier legal solution that had to do with the dead-line, in accordance with the Law on a Temporary Takeover and Management of Property?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph 1 of Article 7, the contracting parties confirmed and they obliged themselves that they would implement the provision of the unalienable right of the owner to take possession of his or her property. That is to say, if the owner returns and wishes to have the property restituted, that this be allowed. And there is an addition which was new as compared to the laws, and that was the right to just compensation. Namely, in accordance with the general principles of international law, the agreement says that if, for whatever reason, it was impossible for the owner to exercise his or her right, that then he certainly had the right to a just compensation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us look a bit further down on the next page of this document where, in paragraph -- which is the first on the page, and that's paragraph 5, reads the following: "Each contracting party shall guarantee the same legal protection to the property of physical and legal persons having the citizenship of the other party, that is, being seated in the territory of the other party, as the one enjoyed by its own citizens, that is, its legal persons." And further on, it reads in the next paragraph: "Within six months from the date of entry into force of the present agreement, the contracting parties shall conclude an agreement on compensation for all destroyed, damaged, or lost property. Such agreement shall define the procedures for the realisation of the right to fair compensation, which shall not include court proceedings." It seems, Ms. Bagic, that the agreement also went one step further as compared to the Law on the Temporary Takeover of property, especially in terms of the fair compensation for property that was destroyed and also in terms of the protection of the property of both physical and legal persons. Can you please comment on this, in brief?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It did go one step further, and I think that paragraph 5 is quite clear. It guarantees that the treatment of property of physical and legal persons will be equal, equal for everyone regardless of the country from which they are coming. This agreement on the normalisation of relations, and this includes paragraphs 5 and 6, by contrast with the Law on the Takeover of Property which relates to the property of physical persons, provides these guarantees also for the property of legal persons. What I feel the need to emphasise is that in this agreement on the normalisation of relations, the commissions that were set up for the purpose of this met regularly. They dealt with the issues of the property of physical persons, the property of refugees, an exchange of informations with lists of persons, and enabling people to restitute their property. I wanted to mention this because the purpose of the agreement and in particular of Article 6 was more extensive than the decree and law that we were talking until now; namely, the purpose was to conclude an agreement that would also relate to all destroyed, damaged, or lost property and colloquially it was called the agreement on war damage. The fact is that until the agreement was reached -- the agreement was never reached, and the commissions stopped working. One of the reasons could be that later on, as is well known, all the former countries that were formed after the break-up of the Yugoslavia reached the agreement on succession, which regulates under Annex G the issue of this property.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us look together at the document D425 now. And to give the temporal context, this agreement between the Republic of Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was concluded in August 1996, that is to say, roughly, one year after Operation Storm, and it regulated the issues that we have just discussed. In the meantime, in the Republic of Croatia, certain procedures were initiated, and they had to do with the implementation of the Law on the Temporary Takeover on property. And some of these proceedings ended up before the constitutional court of the Republic of Croatia, and this had to do with the role of the constitutional court which you described to us in your introduction. Now I'm showing you a decision of the constitutional Court dating the 25th of September, 1997, so a year after the agreement was concluded, and this discussion has to do with the Law on Temporary Takeover and Management of certain property. Ms. Bagic, you are familiar with this decision, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you please briefly interpret this decision of the constitutional court and its importance.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that this was an important decision, because it had to do with the complex issue of ownership and the limits that the law allowed on how to limit it. The constitutional court, acting on the proposal of several parties, initiated the procedure to establish the validity of the Law on Temporary Takeover and Management of certain property. In its decision, the constitutional Court, because these were the proposals --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Please excuse me. You mentioned that the procedure was initiated by certain persons, including --

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: That was the State Prosecutor of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what this function is, as this part of your answer was not interpreted.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. The state attorney is the institution that most closely relates to the ombudsman function. In some western European countries that have this institution, his task is to protect the rights and interests of the citizens, if he believes that they have been violated or jeopardised by some activities of any authorities. So the constitutional court assessed the constitutionality of the law as a whole and also of some of its particular provisions, and the guiding principle was what the proposing parties mentioned in their proposals. While making the decision about the constitutionality of the law as a whole, because that was the primary issue, it took into account primarily the goals and the purpose of this law in the context of the of the relevant provisions of the constitution and also the convention rights, because the European Convention was part of our internal legal system. So deciding on the constitutionality of the law as a whole, finding that the purpose of this law was temporary management of the property for the sake of its protection in the light of the extraordinary circumstances extant at the time when so much of this property was abandoned, on the one hand; and, on the other hand, that there was a necessity and a need to protect this property on the one hand and also to accommodate a huge number of expelled persons and refugees. The constitutional court established that the law as a whole is not unconstitutional, that is to say that it did not violate the constitutional principles under Article 14 and 50 -- Article 50, paragraph 2 of the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia and also the European Convention, especially Protocol 1 additional to the European Convention which relates to property. If you allow me to say, the constitutional court at the time addressed individual provisions and their constitutionality. The constitutional court itself, in its ruling, underlined that they failed to review these provisions as well because there were some indications that there were isolated cases of the violation or abuse of this law. Therefore, the constitutional court raised the issue of the definition of abandoned property and the limits imposed on the temporary uses, and they reviewed these provisions as well. The constitutional court found out that in light of all the then-prevailing conditions in which these norms were adopted and the reasons underlying this adoption, these provisions were also not contrary to the constitution, and they also met all the requirements from Article 50, paragraph 2 of the constitution. The law -- the constitutional court reviewed this -- these provisions within the time-frame, and they took into account its temporary nature. They said that with the passage of time, if the conditions continued to exist, these provisions might be -- continued to be implemented, there will be a need then for them to be reviewed and revised. However, in their further analysis of other provisions, the constitutional court found that some of them were unconstitutional and it rescinded these provisions. These rescinded provisions are Article 8 of the decree and the law. Article 8 of the law imposed a ban on the owner to dispose of his or her property while it was being temporarily used which means that he was not allowed to sell it or swap it or to do anything with it. Although the law itself, according to the constitutional court, was in line with the constitution, they nevertheless decided that this kind of limitation of the ownership rights while it was temporarily used by somebody else without any compensation is not in line with Article 50, paragraph 1 of the constitution, and this provision was also revoked. Also, Article 9, paragraph 2 of the law, as well as paragraph 4 of Article 11, were rescinded, which stipulates that while the property is under temporary management, the temporary user cannot be evicted. Therefore, even when the decision on the use is revoked, he cannot be evicted before he is found an appropriate accommodation. The court found that this kind of procedure was permissible, but preventing the owner to return to its property without setting a time-limit, they found to be unconstitutional, and they also rescinded. Also, Article 11, paragraph 2, which was the amended provision which stipulated that the restitution and the use shall be governed by the agreement between Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, but the court rescinded this, only the portion that referred to the citizens of Croatia who went to live in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or Bosnia and Herzegovina, having found that that would constitute discrimination against other citizens. And according to Article 32 of the constitution, all citizens are entitled to chose where they are going to live. That is why the constitutional court found that this was constitutionally permissible, but, nevertheless, it decided to rescind certain provisions from the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have a slight problem in the translation of the function that the witness mentioned, that is, the function of the Public State Prosecutor. It was translated as the Public State Prosecutor. However, the witness explained that the public defender function is something like an ombudsman. And it was translated in the same way in the ruling of the constitutional court that you see on the right-hand side of your screens. I am saying this just for the record. Can we now look at document D424, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, time-wise, we see that this constitutional court's decision was taken in September. And we see that the Croatian parliament adopted a law on -- to rescind the Law on Temporary Confiscation and Control of certain property. It says that as regards the procedures relating to temporary use and management of property governed by the Law on Temporary Use and Management of Property will -- it will apply a programme of return of refugees and displaced persons. Therefore, this programme of the return basically supercedes this law. Can you please explain to us the motives that the legislators were driven by in adopting this enactment?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Well, the intention was to make the whole process of return as effective as possible. That meant that the procedures relating to the return of citizens and the procedures for restitution of property should be governed in -- should be defined in more detail, should become more practical and pragmatical, and should provide a more simple implementation. This will make it more clear for all those who were applying for the protection of their rights under this document. In cooperation with the international community, we decided that we should adopt a document that would not be a law but, rather, a programme, and that would be a better way to accomplish this goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, I would just say that we are going to ask for the certification of this document, because in the English translation in e-court it says that it is the Law on the Temporary Confiscation. Let us now look at document D428, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Law on the Temporary Takeover was not in force any longer, and it says that all these procedures will be governed or will be part of the programme of return of refugees and displaced persons. And this programme, we can see now on our screens, as document D428. And it was adopted in June 1998. In item 5, we see that the government has drafted this programme in cooperation with the UN agency and with the support of the OSCE. In other words, the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at item 10 of this document, which is on page 3 in the Croatian text. I'm sorry, item -- actually, page 4 in Croatian, item 9 in Croatian; and in English, page 4, item 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The persons with Croatian papers who are owners of property in Republic of Croatia, in whose property other people are temporarily housed, can apply and report to town or municipal housing commissions and file requests for restitution. So this is what it says under item 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 7 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the English version to see, let us say that we are talking here about people in whose property other people are living; may approach city and municipal housing commissions with requests for restitution of their property; the housing commission shall, within five days, inform the owner in writing about the status of their property; and on the basis of proof of ownership, the housing commission shall, within seven days, make a decision overruling the decision on temporary use and shall request of the temporary occupant to vacate the facilities. On the next page we see what happens if the temporary user fails to vacate the property. Then the housing commission shall file a complaint. So this is this programme of return with the deadlines stipulated where the burden of the procedure is on the housing commission, including the filing of complaint and filing charges, actually. Why did the government decide to adopt this solution?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: This covers various situations regarding the returnees. The portion that you read refers to the situation that relates to the Law on the Takeover and Temporary Use of Property. It confirms that the owner is at any time free to come and ask for restitution. By setting up these time limits, we wanted to establish a structure for the owner, once he comes back, to re-acquire his property as soon as possible. Unlike some previous solutions provided in the law, this decision that rescinds the decision issued to the temporary users says that, quite clearly, that the temporary user shall vacate the property within a certain period of time. Now the question arises: What happens if the temporary user fails to comply with this request? Then it will be referred to a court of law. The owner is, at all times, allowed to request the temporary user to vacate his property. However, having in mind that we are talking about the property that had been under the temporary administration by the government for the reasons that we explained earlier, it was believed that the state also has an obligation to initiate court proceedings through housing commissions, ensure to vacate the property, and ensure that the rightful owner will gain his ownership or get restitution. Another reason was, dare I say, a pragmatic one, because the owners are people who always need legal assistance, and if they once embark on legal proceedings, it always take a long time. There is also an issue of the jurisdiction of the courts that used to be in the occupied territories. There were either no judges in those courts or there were no land registers there. That did not make it possible for these proceedings to be conducted in an expeditious way. That is why yes thought that housing commissions are better placed to deal with these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just one question more before we break. It says here that the court is going to resort to an abridged proceedings, that the decision will be final, and that the decision will not stay the execution of that decision, that is to say, the restitution of property. Is that consistent with what you said about the role of the government?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, because that was both in the interests of the government and of the owner, for him to get restitution as soon as possible. And for that purpose, certain provisions have been transferred and allowed to be conducted in a speedy way and that any appeal will not stay the execution of this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, your last words, I couldn't hear them because translation was still continuing. So, therefore, I missed you -- but I take it that you wanted to suggest to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break, and we will resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bagic, in your testimony, on several occasions, you mentioned the Court for Human Rights, the European Court in Strasbourg. Briefly, in relation to Croatian legislation, can you tell us what procedure needs to be followed for someone to be able to apply to the court for Human Rights in Strasbourg?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: For someone to apply or complain to the court in Strasbourg, in individual cases, all domestic legal means must have been exhausted. That is to say, all regular legal remedies must have been exhausted in Croatia. After a first-instance court decision, an appeal must be submitted, and a request for revision must be made after a second-instance decision to the constitutional court --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to the supreme court in Croatia as the highest court instance. Such a person also needs to invoke protection before the constitutional court in Croatia, after which, a complaint can be made to the European Court for Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to the 65 ter document 3D00180.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will show you a decision by the Court for Human Rights in the case Kunic versus Croatia. First of all, are you familiar with this decision of the European Court?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could we go through the -- through a part of this decision together?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 64 in the electronic version; it is page 12 in the English. And in the Croatian version it is 3D00-1185, paragraph 64.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The title of that paragraph is: "The Court's Assessment." In paragraph 65 -- sorry, let's start with paragraph 64. It is states therein that: "In the court's view, there has indisputably been an interference with the applicant's right to property as his house was allocated for use to another person and he was unable to use it for a prolonged period of time." The Law on Temporary Taking Over of Property was enforced in this case. In item 65 it is stated: "The court further notes that the applicant was not deprived of his title. Therefore, the interference complained of constituted a control of use of property within the meaning of second paragraph of Article 1 of Protocol I." In paragraph 66 it is stated, and I will ask for your comment: "The court considers that it does not have to decide whether the very fact of giving the applicant's house to a third person was justified under Article 1 of Protocol I to the convention. Even assuming so, the situation became significantly different once the applicant instituted the relevant proceedings for repossession of his house, thereby making it clear that he needed it for himself and his family. In those proceedings, the domestic authorities recognised the applicant's right to repossession, issued an order ordering the temporary tenant to move out, hence instituting the procedure for returning the property. It only needs to be established whether this practice was contrary to Article 1." It is clear from this quotation that the European Court for Human Rights itself believed that it was not in dispute, that by virtue of the decision of Croatian government the rightful owner was not denied his property rights. This tallies with what you are already said. Can you provide any further comments?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Indeed, it corresponds to what we have been discussing so far. It seems to me that it also invokes the position of the constitutional court in their decision of 1997, which I mentioned previously. The constitutional court did not find the law to be unconstitutional, although it revoked certain of its provisions because they did not meet the standards of limitation of property rights as envisage the under the constitution. In this individual case, this was further elaborated in some decisions of the European Court for Human Rights, including this one. I believe it is clearly stated that this was no case of taking away property rights in the sense of Protocol I, Article 1. The legitimate goal of the governmental action was within the law. However, a new moment is introduced by the European Court and that is the question whether the realisation of such a procedure met the high standards it had to. This was a natural evolution which evolved from the law through the implementation of the programme and onwards. And in individuals cases, it needed further monitoring. Some of those cases were brought before the European Court. This new standard is set in a number of decisions including this one. It is a question of whether, in individual cases, because of the prolonged period during which the property in question was not being returned, whether such instances were against Article 1, Protocol I.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is the decision of the 11th of January, 2007?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm -- I apologise for the interruption. I just -- I should have objected earlier, but I didn't get a chance before the witness began her answer. The question was: "It is clear from this quotation that the European Court for Human Rights itself believes that it was not in dispute that by virtue of the decision of the Croatian government the rightful owner was not denied his property rights." And I just want to put on record that I don't believe that's a fair characterisation of what the Court was saying here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the Court says that the applicant was not deprived of his title. That's what --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... title, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... even without -- yes, even without any further explanation of the witness, this Court is -- this Chamber is able to read the text in its original version and ... Now, I nevertheless have one question to put in relation to the interpretation, apart from whether or not it is for the witness to -- to interpret the decisions of the European Court of Human Rights. But since she has done so, I'm trying to seek some clarification. Ms. Bagic, I read part of your answer: "The legitimate goal of the governmental action was within the law," you said. What governmental action did you have in mind there? Was that adopting the law, or did you have in mind temporarily depriving this applicant from the -- from enjoying his property? Which did you have in mind when you said "The legitimate goal of the governmental action was within the law"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, but I was not aware of having used "the legitimate goal of governmental action." It may be do to interpretation in different languages. In any case, what I had in mind, the legitimate goal, were the regulations put in force by the Croatian government. That is to say, the Law on Temporarily Taking Away Property and its return. Those documents and such regulations were legitimate. They were implemented with a legitimate goal in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Where do we find that in this decision? I'm not saying that it's to be found nowhere, But where do we find it in this decision; can you please tell us? Do you have a copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. It is before me. I have a copy of this decision. It is not stated in the decision itself. It can be found in another decision, and I felt free to expand and interpret. I believe it is in the Radanovic case decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could then, please, the Radanovic decision be put on the screen so that we find it in there. I'm just trying to find out what's the basis of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that was my next step. I will just try to -- I will just try to produce the Saratlic decision where the legitimate goal was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- if the witness tells us that the goal is found in the Radanovic decision and if then in your next comment you say in what decision it is to be found, then that is not exactly what we expect you to do. The Saratlic decision is not the decision the witness mentioned, is it? She talked about the Radanovic decision, which is a different one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour, I'm aware of this, but I had the impression that the witness says, "I believe it is in Radanovic case," so I simply believed that the witness was not sure whether this was really in Radanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then you were in a position to tell her that it is in another decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I'm sorry if I interfere in an inappropriate way, but that was my next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. But before I proceed, I would like to enter this document into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we need case law of international courts into ... I mean, once I read it in the statement of the witness, the first thing I did is to look in HUDOC where to find it, although I must admit that I have difficulties in finding some of these decisions. Although not this one. This is easily accessible on the Internet, that is, Kunic versus Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, I am ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber considers that there's no need to have this case law, if easily accessible through the normal search engines of the European Court on Human Rights to have it in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Can we go to 3D00182 next, please. It is the decision of the Saratlic case of the European Court in Strasbourg. This decision is dated the 24th of October, 2006. In the English, can we go to page 6, paragraph 2, please. In the Croatian version, the first paragraph on the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is stated as follows: "As to the conduct of the administrative authorities in ensuring the repossession of the house in question to the applicant, the Court observes, firstly, that the State had a legitimate interest in housing displaced persons in the property left behind by persons who left Croatia during the war. Furthermore, the system which allows such persons to remain in the occupied property before they have been provided with adequate housing is not in itself in contradiction with the guarantees contained in Article 1 of Protocol 1, providing that it ensures sufficient safeguards for the protection of the applicant's property rights." Ms. Bagic, this part of the Court's decision is before you. Could you please comment on it, to the extent you are familiar with this case?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: In this specific case before me, that is to say, the Saratlic case, it seems to me, although I only have this excerpt before me, that it involved an applicant which -- or who submitted no official applications for the repossession of the property involved or to be compensated for the use of that house. The European Court basically found his application to be unfounded. The Court also specified what it did in the paragraph you just read out concerning the housing of displaced persons in the property of those who had left the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us go to the next case, which is the Kostic case. We have another decision of the European Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can we, perhaps, Mr. Mikulicic, first ask the witness to explain why the case was dismissed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This case was dismissed because the applicant, I believe, had previously sold his property, although he was using it. He sold it through another person whom he gave a letter of appointment or authorised --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Power of attorney.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and that person concluded the contract on his behalf. However, that could not be proven. The person authorised to sell the house when the seizure procedure was instituted, stating that there were no bases for any further proceedings in that respect. In my view, the European Court for Human Rights in the particular circumstances believed that this could not be in violation of Protocol 1, Article 1, and the property rights specified therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it was mainly the failure to seek the enforcement order to be carried out, an enforcement order that was there, and the failure of the applicant to seek compensation which finally resulted in a decision that the application was manifestly ill-founded, rather than to have any substantial decision on any action or activity of the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me, if I be allowed to interpret this decision, that the European Court did not deem it necessary to assess the activities of the Croatian government in this specific case but only in terms of the length of the procedure for the seizure, and it deemed that it lasted an appropriate time, that it did not last too long. And apart from that, it did not assess the activities of the Croatian authorities, precisely because previously in this specific case, the applicant had possession of his property and had sold it. So this is why I suppose he did not ask for compensation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that was a disputed matter, whether he had given his consent to apparently a signed document. But let's proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 3D00200. That is the decision of the Court in Strasbourg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way, this decision is not easily accessible through the HUDOC system because it -- even if you give the number of the case, it gives no response. Therefore it might be a good idea to have this one in evidence, although, exceptionally, because usually case law which is accessible to the parties should not be tendered or admitted into evidence. But the decision of Saratlic versus Croatia, Mr. Registrar, the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document under 65 ter 3D182 will be admitted into evidence as Exhibit D1912. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1912 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Let us look at the decision in the case Kostic versus the Republic of Croatia. And if we could please see page 6 in the English version. It seems to me I don't even have the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And here it reads, in the second paragraph reads -- sorry, the third paragraph is the one I find interesting. It reads as follows. I will quote in English: [In English] "... that the applicant had a final judgement confirming his ownership of the house in question, and ordering the eviction of the temporary occupants."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move on to the next page. That's page 7, which reads -- and this is the decision of the Court. It is the fifth paragraph from the bottom of the page up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] "The Court notes that the Programme for Return equally applies to all persons who return to Croatia, irrespective of their ethnic origin, and that there is no indication that the applicant was discriminated against in any respect." [Interpretation] Ms. Bagic, what I'm interested in here is how you understand the part of the decision in which the Court concludes that the Programme for Return was not discriminatory in terms of ethnic origin. Could you please, to the best of your knowledge and recollection, comment on this section of the position of the Court in Strasbourg?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: I will try to tell you how I understand this part of the decision of the European Court. As one can see, it relates to the application of the Programme for the Return of Refugees and Displaced Persons. This programme elaborated in detail, in a number of items, various situations relating to the return of refugees and expelled persons and also the fact whether they had or did not have the documents testifying to their Croatian citizenship; what was the procedure for them to obtain such documents, if they did not have them; and also, as regards whether they had any property in Croatia, whether it was vacant or temporarily occupied. It can be concluded that the Court refers to the fact that the applicant in his application to the European Court believed and claimed that in the application of the programme there was discrimination against him because of his ethnic origin. And the Court established that the programme applied equally to all persons returning to Croatia, so the procedure was the same for everyone, regardless of their ethnic origin. That is to say, what they were by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When we started our discussion today, Ms. Bagic, you told us what your positions were in the state administration, specifically in the Ministry of Justice, especially in the difficult time when we had practically a state of war in Croatia. During your work in the state administration and the Ministry of Justice, did you ever receive an order or participate in a discussion or were present during a discussion which, in any way, one ethnic community in the Republic of Croatia or members of an ethnic community or a religious community would be discriminated in any way whatsoever? Did you ever, in any discussions relating to the adoption of decrees and laws, take into account such goals, or were those goals in any way suggested to you?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: During my work in the ministry and when I participated in the work of various Working Groups and delegations as part of my duties and the positions I had in the Ministry, I did not take part nor was I directed by a goal that would discriminate citizens on the basis of their ethnicity nor did we ever receive such orders myself or any of the colleagues that worked with me as part of these Working Groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mikulicic, when you refer to the -- I think you said judgement in the Kostic case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Maybe my word was "decision," but that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes. Because there was -- yes, let me just check. Because we should clearly distinguish between the decision on admissibility in this case, which he apparently refer to in the judgement in this case which was a judgement in which a friendly settlement was put on paper. And that, of course, was limited to the portion which was declared admissible. I'm looking at the other Defence teams, whether there's any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We don't have any questions for this witness, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions from the Cermak Defence. Gotovina Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. Ms. Gustafson, are you ready to start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Bagic.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to start just by asking you some preliminary questions about your preparation to testify in this case. Before coming here today to testify, have you seen any of this trial or have you followed any of the proceedings in this trial?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: No, I did not particularly follow the proceedings, except for what was broadcast or published in the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you've explained that the date of your interview with the Markac Defence was the 23rd of October, 2009. When did you first receive communications from the Markac Defence about testifying in this case, or providing a statement?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markac's Defence first contacted me by phone and asked me and proposed that I be a Defence witness in connection with the Law on the Temporary Takeover and Management of Property. I accepted this in principle, because I believed that whoever knows anything about certain topics has a duty to testify about that. And after that, we met for the first time at Mr. Mikulicic's office on the said day - that was the 23rd of October - in order to draft my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And other than the telephone call, the 23rd of October meeting, and the meeting I understand you had yesterday with the Markac Defence, have you had any other communications with them about any of the -- any matters of substance in this case?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: No, there were no other contacts, except that after we met on the 23rd at Mr. Mikulicic's office, when we talked in more detail what would be the subject of my testimony and we agreed about the draft of my statement, as far as I remember, I think I had to rush and I had no more time, so after that, Mr. Rendulic came to my office in the constitutional court. I think it was on the 29th of October. And the idea was for me to review my statement, to check the dates, and the specific Articles, possible incorrect use of terms, and for me to sign it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And do you know how the Markac Defence learned that you were involved in drafting the property law? You explained that they raised it with you.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, and I didn't ask them that. But it was no secret, considering that for years before I moved to the constitutional court, I worked for the Ministry of Justice and the government administration, so it was known what sort of work I had been doing. I was also a member of the parliament committees. And as the deputy minister, I was also a member of various commissions and groups that dealt with this kind of problems. So I suppose that this motivated the Defence to get in touch with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you ever informed about the nature or contents of the testimony of any other witness in this case?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like do move on and ask you some questions about your role in the Ministry of Justice at the time of the events in question. Can you explain to the Court, please, more specifically what your duties were in the Ministry of Justice, specifically in 1995, in the latter half of 1995? What -- what exactly was your function in terms of your day-to-day duties?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: I will try. Since 1995, around mid-1995, around the 20th -- at some point in June in 1995, I was appointed the secretary of the Ministry of Justice. So in the first half of 1995, I worked in the administration for property law. I was an assistant of the manager of this administration at the time, or the chief. And then in June 1995, I was appointed secretary of the Ministry of Justice. And in 1997, in March of that year, I was appointed deputy minister of justice. In the administration for property law as the assistant chief, I reviewed the files that were produced by my colleagues who were also working in this administration. I was also a member of the Working Groups, which drafted and prepared regulations relating to the area of property law; for example, these were the Law on Property, the Law on Land Registry, the Law on Compensation for property that was seized -- I apologise. The Law on the Compensation for property seized under the Yugoslav Communist regime. Also the Law on Asset Seizure and the law on -- the Law on Media, and let me not enumerate any further. I also went to the sessions of the government of the Republic of Croatia, and I participated in the work of the professional bodies. These were the so-called coordinations of the government. They harmonise the documents prepared by various ministries within the remit of their work before these documents are submitted to the government. I was also a member of certain commissions. For example, for settling the relations with the church and also the -- setting relations with --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise, Ms. Bagic, perhaps I can direct your attention a little more specifically. You mentioned attending sessions of the government and you were shown one session of the government that you said you didn't think you attended. How often did you attend government sessions?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, I would like to clarify that. I said that I did not -- or actually I didn't say that I attended the sessions of the government, but, rather, the meetings of professional bodies of the government that worked on dove-tailing the documents prepared by various ministries in order for them to be submitted later to the government. The period of time that I'm talking about, that is, when I was the assistant head of the property law department, by virtue of my post, I could not have attended the sessions of the government. I could only do that when I became deputy minister. And I became deputy minister in March of 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So while you were secretary of the Ministry of Justice between 1995 and 1997 you did not attend any government sessions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me for the period in which I was the deputy minister of justice?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you to confirm that I understand your testimony correctly. That while you were secretary of the Ministry of Justice between 1995 and 1997, that you did not attend any government sessions. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: While I was the ministry secretary, no, I didn't attend the sessions of the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And as secretary of the Ministry of Justice, who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: To the minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And how frequent were your contacts with the minister? And if could you briefly describe what kinds of contacts you had with him when you were the secretary of the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Our contacts were as if and when necessary. We had normal communication, we discussed and agreed who was going where or not going somewhere. The minister would ask me to come to his office for giving me instructions to prepare something or if I wanted to tell him something. It is difficult to say anything about the frequency of our meetings. Sometimes it happened that we didn't see each other for two days, and then we would meet and spend two or three hours together.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did you meet with him and have -- or have communications with him about the substance of the property law that you have been -- the Law on Temporary Takeover that was discussed in your testimony? Just to be clear, that would be Minister Miroslav Separovic at the time.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: I suppose that we did. The minister was not officially a member of the group who worked on it, but I suppose - I cannot remember at the moment - but that was the usual procedure with every law, that when a law is nearly finished, we could contact the minister; brief him on the content of the law; ask for his suggestions; if he had any regarding amendment; and that was done, because, when he went to the government or to the parliament, he would, before that, summon all of us to furnish him with all the details so that he can prepare his expose either at the government or before the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in terms of the Law on the Temporary Takeover of Property, you can't remember specifically at this time what the procedure was in terms of Minister Separovic's involvement?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: The procedure that involved the participation of the minister in the preparation of the law was always the same or similar. In other words, the minister was someone who, at the final stage, on behalf of the Ministry, and the member of the government, goes before the government to explain the details of the law. If he manages to get the endorsement by the government, then this same minister would present it and defend it before the parliament on behalf of the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you mentioned a Working Group that was involved in preparing the Law on the Temporary Takeover of Property. Were all those people from the Ministry of Justice, or were there people from outside the Ministry involved in drafting that law in your Working Group?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: Also involved were other people as well. This law was done by a group of lawyers from the Ministry of Justice, the Department for Property Law. However, also involved in this process were our colleagues from the Department of Legislature. We probably also contacted people from the judiciary, that is, from the public prosecutor's office as it was called at the time, and probably some colleagues from the Ministry for Public Works and Reconstruction, which was directly responsible for providing accommodation of refugees and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Was that the Ministry that was known at the time as the Ministry for Reconstruction and Development; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: I suppose so. The ministries changed names very often, so I cannot say with any degree of certainty how it was called at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And aside from your contacts with Minister Separovic, did you have any other direct communications with any other government ministers during the time you were the secretary to the Ministry of Justice? And I'm concerned particularly with the period in 1995.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any -- any specific contacts with any minister or anyone from the government. It may happen that the Ministry would convene a meeting or it could happen that I accompanied the minister at a meeting with another Ministry where other ministers would also be present. But any specific contacts between them and myself, I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, I'm looking at the clock. Would this be a suitable moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then before we adjourn, Mr. Mikulicic, when I said that the Saratlic decision was not easily accessible, it was my mistake, because in the search engine you will have to specifically include decisions from the Court, apart from seeking for judgements. And, therefore, I suggest to you that in line with the general rule that easily accessible case law is not admitted into evidence, that we vacate D1912 and advise everyone not to leave out the decisions of the European Court of Human Rights. And for the transcriber, the HUDOC system is H-U-D-O-C, which is the database from the European Court of Human Rights, easily accessible through the Internet. Any objections, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections. It's all right with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D1912 is vacated. Ms. Bagic, we'll adjourn for the day. We would like to see you back tomorrow morning, the 12th of January at 9.00 in this same Courtroom. And I would like to instruct you that you should not speak to anyone about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given already today or testimony still to be given tomorrow. We adjourn until the 12th of January, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of January, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
